name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
title: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
answer: Asking data questions in plain language covers interfaces that turn a user's everyday wording into an executable query over structured data, such as a database, a warehouse, or a spreadsheet. It sits in quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the answer is only useful if the path from question to result can be inspected and repeated. The practice includes text-to-SQL, semantic parsing, conversational business intelligence, and large language model assistants that draft queries for review. It is not a replacement for understanding the data model, and it is not a general chat feature, because the output must run against real tables and return a verifiable result.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Asking data questions in plain language covers interfaces that turn a user's everyday wording into an executable query over structured data, such as a database, a warehouse, or a spreadsheet. It sits in quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the answer is only useful if the path from question to result can be inspected and repeated. The practice includes text-to-SQL, semantic parsing, conversational business intelligence, and large language model assistants that draft queries for review. It is not a replacement for understanding the data model, and it is not a general chat feature, because the output must run against real tables and return a verifiable result.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a database or warehouse that can execute queries, a semantic layer or metadata catalog that names tables, columns, and metrics, and a client such as a notebook, a business intelligence tool, or a chat pane. A language model or a smaller semantic parser translates the question, often with retrieval over schema descriptions and example queries to keep the mapping grounded. Execution happens in a controlled environment with read-only credentials, query timeouts, and resource limits, so a poorly formed question cannot scan an entire warehouse by accident. Reproducibility depends on versioned data, saved query text, and a recorded environment, which is why SQL, Python, and notebook files remain the durable artifacts even when the question was asked in plain language.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical session starts with a question, then the system inspects the available schema, proposes a query, and either runs it or asks a clarifying question when a term is ambiguous. The generated query is checked against tests, row counts, or known reference answers before the result is shown, and the user can refine the question in follow-up turns. Teams build evaluation sets of question and query pairs, measure execution accuracy and result correctness, and track failures such as wrong joins, missing filters, or misread date ranges. The final artifact is usually the query and its result set, not the chat transcript, so the analysis can be rerun when the data changes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on access control, because a plain language interface can expose rows that the asker is not entitled to see if permissions are not enforced at the query layer. Provenance requires keeping the original question, the generated query, the schema version, the data snapshot, and the model version together, so a result can be audited later. The site's own library holds 135 research papers and 12233 claims extracted from research works, and it links to original papers rather than a search tool, which is a useful pattern for tracing a claim back to its source. Teams also guard against hallucinated columns, ambiguous metric definitions, and prompt injection through data values, and they log every query for review.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter integration between natural language front ends and the semantic layers, notebooks, and BI tools that already hold the definitions of metrics and dimensions. Expect more agentic workflows that propose a query, run it, inspect the result, and revise, but with human approval at the point where a number leaves the sandbox. Evaluation will mature around reproducible benchmarks that test not only whether a query runs but whether it answers the intended question on a known dataset. The plain language layer will likely remain a convenience, while the durable record stays in version-controlled SQL, Python, and metadata, so that quantitative work can be checked and reused.
